text: Eighty-four minutes is a short leash for a western, and the brevity does the arguing: the continent gets crossed at the pace of someone with no idea how large it is. That someone is seventeen, Scottish, and travelling on an infatuation — a woman is out there in the territory, and he intends to arrive at her. The gunman who attaches himself to the errand has reasons the boy does not examine, which is its own kind of romance. John Maclean lets the genre's furniture stand where it always stands, horses and distances and men with rifles, while the actual subject stays one young head full of a picture that reality has not yet been consulted about. It took the World Cinema Dramatic grand jury prize at Sundance, an award for a film that treats the frontier as something a boy walks across toward a girl.

Ordinary is a word people accept about themselves for years and then, one morning, do not. The woman here is introduced as an ordinary one, which is both how such lives get filed and how they are often lived: days alike enough that a decision can assemble itself behind them without anyone at the kitchen table noticing. Dominic Savage spends a hundred and two minutes on one person and one choice. That is a narrow allotment, and it rules out incident as a support; what remains is the arithmetic by which someone works out that the arrangement she has been holding together is also hers to put down. Nothing in the premise promises she is right, or that the life on the far side is better than the one behind her. The interest lies in watching a decision stop being hypothetical.

The father speaks Danish and the desert does not care what he says or how far he has come. He has brought his daughter across the world to a place that goes unnamed, and the journey is the whole plot: two people, a horizon, and the growing difficulty of saying where the map stops. Lisandro Alonso accepts the western label and honours half of its promise — the open country is there, the assurance that open country leads somewhere is withdrawn. A hundred and ten minutes at that pace asks for a particular kind of attention and repays it in kind: light on sand, an animal heard before it is seen, distance measured by the time it takes to cross. What holds the film taut is domestic and simple. A man a long way from home is responsible for a girl, and the terrain was not arranged with either of them in mind.

A group of people back from a war, working out how to live beside one another: that is the whole event, and it runs two hours and three minutes. Italy has just been reassembled as a country, and the men and women here are assembling something smaller and harder — terms between the sexes, between generations, between neighbours who spent the war in opposing political camps and now share the same ruined ground. What they are trying to put behind them is not only the war but the ordinary hardship underneath it: hunger, fear, the difficulty of getting through a winter. Jean-Marie Straub gives such a community the full length of a film and declines to turn it into a plot. Nothing arrives from outside to settle it. The drama is procedural: who speaks, who is owed, who agrees to stay.

The dogs are tied up and the people are flown out, and every minute afterwards proceeds from that gap. A storm shuts the Antarctic base; the rescue meant to follow is called off in a decision taken somewhere else, and the trainer who left the team behind spends six months looking for someone willing to pay for a return trip. Frank Marshall splits two hours between the two situations — a man working phones and sponsors in the world, eight animals working out food and weather at the bottom of it. It is made for families, which mostly means the guilt is legible and the landscape is photographed with affection. What gives it more weight than its shape suggests is the plainness of the arrangement: a promise was made to animals, and animals cannot be told that circumstances have changed.

The rule of the evening is that only the good parts get told. Two friends, back from separate trips to the same seaside town, trade fond memories over drinks; neither realises they were there at the same time, among the same handful of people, who behave rather differently depending on which man is doing the remembering. Hong Sang-soo runs this for just under two hours and never lets the two accounts meet at the table. The comedy is in the gap, and so is whatever is unkind about it, since a man's flattering version of himself is funny only as long as it stays at arm's length. Flashback here is not a device for explaining anyone. It is a way of showing that two people can spend a week in one small town and come home with entirely different towns.

A move is supposed to be a solution, and for a while the two people in this one agree to treat it as one. The father takes a new job. The daughter enters a school where everyone already knows everyone, which is the harder assignment of the two. Michel Franco keeps them in separate daylight hours and returns them to each other in the evening, where what they left behind goes unmentioned by something like mutual consent. That silence is not neglect; it is the arrangement that made the move possible. A hundred and three minutes gives it room to hold and room to be tested, and the film's unhurried attention is what makes the testing visible — a girl adjusting, a father not asking, a household in which the cost of starting over is paid on separate schedules.

Three genres are declared and none of them gives way: horror, romance, science fiction, all of it on the Italian coast. A young American has come there in the middle of a personal collapse, not with a plan but with a departure, and what he finds is a woman worth staying for. The courtship proceeds in the usual currency — meals, walks, evasions — with one party keeping to herself something considerably older than the town. Justin Benson gives the romance its time, which is the film's real decision: a hundred and ten minutes is long for horror and about right for two people learning each other's habits. The pressure builds less from what is hidden than from the ordinary problem of when to say it, and to whom, and what a person is expected to do with the answer.

A fine arts student and a bartender: the two jobs are doing more work than they appear to. One keeps studio hours, the other works while the bars are open, so the relationship is a scheduling problem before it is anything else. Lee Hyun-ju gives the two women ninety-nine minutes and no external plot to hurry them along — they meet, they become involved, and then they have to conduct that involvement inside lives already crowded with classmates, deadlines, shifts, and the running question of how much to explain and to whom. The film's attention goes to practical texture: whose room, whose money, whose silence. First attachments are usually filmed as weather. This one is filmed as a set of arrangements negotiated week by week, without a template to work from.

Toni Kurz and Andreas Hinterstoisser went at the north face of the Eiger, and the film keeps their names because the record did. Philipp Stölzl reconstructs the attempt across a hundred and twenty-six minutes, and most of that time is cold, rope, and the arithmetic of turning back. Climbing pictures tend to organise themselves around will; this one is also about kit — what two German climbers had to work with, and how much of a route is settled before anyone touches the rock. The wall is called deadly in every account of it, which is a fact about the mountain and also a fact about why people go. Stölzl seems most interested in the interval before commitment: weather read from below, a decision made in a warm room, the point past which returning is harder than continuing.

Hollywood in the 1930s ran on introductions, and a young man arriving there hoping for work in pictures is really hoping to be introduced. Woody Allen spends ninety-seven minutes among the people who did the introducing: the parties, the restaurants, the loose confederation of the well-placed that the period called café society and that the film treats as a scene and a labour market at once. The love story runs inside that, by design — romance among people who are also one another's professional opportunities, conducted at a volume suitable for overhearing. The comedy sits on the surface and it is genuinely comic. Underneath is the older subject of what proximity to glamour costs, and how briskly the price is agreed to by everyone in the room.
